Promoting the production of methane on the co-digestion of food waste and 
sewage sludge by aerobic pre-treatment 
Lijie Cheng a, Ningbo Gao a,*, Cui Quan a, Hua Chu b, Guojuan Wang b 
a School of Energy and Power Engineering, Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an 710049, China 
b Xi’an Aerospace Chemical Propulsion Co., Ltd, Xi’an 710025, China   
A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
Aerobic pre-treatment 
Food waste (FW) 
Sewage sludge (SS) 
CH4 production 
Substrate formation 
A B S T R A C T   
In this study, methane (CH4) production performance on the co-digestion of food waste (FW) and sewage sludge 
(SS) was compared under non-pretreatment and 6 days aerobic pre-treatment. The results showed that, 
compared with the non-aerobic group, the CH4 productivity increased by nearly 60% through aerobic pre­
treatment. More ammonium was obtained after pre-aeration, providing a suitable growth environment for 
methanogens. After the aerobic pretreatment, proteins and carbohydrates converted into solute protein and 
carbohydrate, which could be easily consumed by microorganisms, concentrations of solute protein and car­
bohydrate were 350 and 667 mg/L in R2 and Pre-R2, respectively. At the same time, aerobic pretreatment 
affected the distribution of microbial community in the system. In the stable stage of Pre-R2, Methanosarcina as 
acetate-utilizing methanogen, became the dominant in the reactor, whose abundance was over 93%. It meant 
after the aerobic pretreatment, the main pathway for methanogenesis was acetotrophy. This study revealed that 
pre-aeration is a simple and desirable strategy for improving the CH4 productivity on the co-digestion of FW and 
SS.   
1. Introduction 
As the main part of municipal solid waste (MSW), the disposal of FW 
has become an urgent issue. The amount of FW is increasing year by 
year. It is reported that 1.3 billion tons of FW has been generated every 
year all over the world [1]. Particularly in China, the rapid increase in 
FW is triggered by population growth and urbanization. More than 
80–110 million tons of FW is produced annually, accounting for 40–60% 
of MSW in China [2]. FW contains high content of organic matter, which 
is easily degraded in a short period of time, thus producing serious 
odors. This also results in breeding mosquitoes and flies, thereby, 
destroying the environment and spreading diseases. Once the leakage 
occurred during the process of FW collection and transportation, it 
would pose threat to the human health and environment [3,4]. The 
traditional technologies for the treatment of food waste are composting, 
incineration and sanitary landfill, but, they are proved to, not only cause 
the loss of chemical values of FW, but also result in secondary pollution, 
like the production of dioxins and 2,3,7,8-tetrachlorodibenzo-p-dioxin 
(2,3,7,8-TCDD), these by-products are toxic to human health [5,6]. 
Anaerobic digestion refers to the process of decomposing biodegradable 
organic matter into biogas by anaerobic microorganism. It is an attrac­
tive technology and holds dual-advantage, i.e., reducing organic waste 
and resulting in energy recovery [7]. 
Due to the abundance of protein, lipids and carbohydrates, food 
waste has been considered to be a potential substrate in the anaerobic 
digestion process for the degradation and production of CH4 [8]. 
Numerous researchers have carried out the anaerobic digestion of food 
waste and found that because of the VFAs accumulation, imbalance of 
C/N ratio, insufficient trace elements in the anaerobic digestion process 
of the food waste, low CH4 yield was obtained [4]. It has been reported 
that when the organic loading rate (OLR) is higher than 2.5 g VS/L/ 
d under thermophilic conditions, single anaerobic digestion of food 
waste failed due to the accumulation of VFAs and ammonia [9]. In order 
to improve the performance of the anaerobic digestion system, an array 
of strategies are proposed, such as adding trace elements [10], pre- 
treatment methods (including sonication pretreatment [11], ionizing 
radiation [12]; mechanical grinding [13]). Although anaerobic diges­
tion performance of food waste can be enhanced by these methods, but, 
most of these methods are costly and it is difficult to apply them 
commercially into the plants. As a popular strategy, co-digestion can

increase the CH4 production yield with following advantage: (1) sup­
plying additional nutrients; (2) allowing for treatment of different 
organic wastes in a single facility; (3) refining the buffer capacity and (4) 
improving the stability of the anaerobic digestion system [14,15]. 
Because of the abundance of microorganisms and micronutrients, SS is 
commonly used as co-substrate for FW [9]. 
Compared with the chemical and physical pre-treatment, aerobic 
pretreatment, as a relatively cheap and easy pre-treatment technology 
(only need to pump oxygen into the system), is favored as an appropriate 
option to stimulate CH4 production from MSW, lignocellulosic biomass 
and SS [16,17]. Ni et al. [18] studied the effect of pre-aeration time on 
CH4 and hydrogen production from municipal solid waste and 
concluded that aerobic pretreatment can significantly improve the 
performance of dry anaerobic digestion, that is, an optimum pre- 
aeration reduced the organic loading and enhanced the buffer capac­
ity of the reactors. The effect of aerobic pretreatment on the CH4 pro­
duction of food waste from different materials (protein, lipids and 
carbohydrate) has also been studied by Rafieenia [19], at a two-stage 
anaerobic digestion process, they found the effect of aerobic pretreat­
ment is greatly related to different feedstock, pre-aeration showed 
positive effects on CH4 production for protein rich and carbohydrate rich 
samples. Gonz´alez-Gonz´alez et al. [20] has showed that aerobic pre­
treatment is profitable for olive oil anaerobic digestion, after 5 days, the 
CH4 yield was 2.4 times higher than untreated and 1.4 times higher than 
7 days aerated treatment. The aerobic pre-treatment can degrade the 
organics of substrates, thus avoiding the overload of organic and pro­
moting the CH4 production. However, there has been no studies focused 
on the same OLR during the digestion process and pre-aerated and non- 
pretreated substrates were introduced as feed in the subsequent anaer­
obic process. In order to reveal the effect of pre-aeration on the sub­
strates, in this research, the natural reoxygenation pretreatment on the 
substrate are investigated in a semi-continuous system without adding 
any additional bacteria. The effects of aerobic pre-treatment on the 
subsequent methanogenesis are also investigated with the pretreated 
and untreated substrate as the raw feed material (the same high loading 
rate in anaerobic digestion stage, OLR = 4 g VS/L/day). In addition, to 
ensure the stability of the anaerobic digestion system under high OLR, 
co-digestion of FW and SS with different ratios are also considered. To 
find out the difference of substrates treated with and without the pre- 
aeration, the fraction of substrates was analyzed. Meanwhile, the mi­
crobial distribution at the final running stage of anaerobic digestion was 
measured. 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. FW and SS 
FW used in this study was collected from the school canteen of Xi’an 
Jiaotong university. Undesirable materials (like tissue, bones and plas­
tics) were manually screened out. In order to get as many diverse in­
gredients as possible, the food waste samples were taken from different 
waste disposal buckets and mixed thoroughly. They were then crushed 
into viscous liquid and stored in a −20 ◦C refrigerator before carrying 
out the experiments. SS came from one of the wastewater treatment 
plants in Xi’an, China. The detailed information about food waste and 
sewage sludge is summarized in Table 1. 
2.2. Inoculum 
The inoculum was obtained from mesophilic anaerobic digester of a 
municipal sludge treatment plant in Dalian, China. The pH of inoculum 
was 7.45 ± 0.12 and total solid (TS) was 68.5 ± 1.6 g/L with a 46.1% 
VS/TS ratio. Prior to the experiment, the inoculum was degassed for 5 
min. 
2.3. Experimental procedure 
The detailed steps of experiment are designed as follows.  
(1) A 6 days natural pre-aeration with different FW:SS ratio of 
substrates.  
(2) The substrate treated by pre-aeration and original substrate were 
used as the feed for the anaerobic digestion process under the 
same OLR. 
2.3.1. Aerobic pre-treatment of substrates 
To compare the substrates with and without aerobic pre-treatment, 
two arrays were performed. Moreover, experiments were also per­
formed with different FW:SS ratio. The pre-treatment array was carried 
out as follows: substrates were prepared at designated ratios (FW(VS):SS 
(VS) = 1:0, 3:1, 1:1, VS calculated). Then, the obtained substrates were 
further diluted to 500 mL (with distilled water) in three identical bea­
kers, respectively, followed by aerobically incubated for 6 days without 
adding any extra microorganism. During the operation period, the in­
door temperature was kept at 30 ± 2 ◦C, beakers were stirred by hand 
every 24 h with a neat glass rod. The substrates after 6 days aerobic pre- 
treatment was used as the feed during the anaerobic digestion process 
and stored in a −20 ◦C refrigerator until their use. 
2.3.2. Semi-continuous anaerobic digestion process 
Semi-continuous anaerobic digestion stage was carried out in a lab­
oratory scale test to evaluate the production of CH4. There are six re­
actors, corresponding to Pre-R1, Pre-R2, Pre-R3, R1, R2, R3, where R1, 
R2, R3 represent substrates without pre-treatment, with proportions of 
FW:SS were 1:0, 3:1, 1:1, respectively. Pre-R1, Pre-R2, Pre-R3 indicate 
that the substrates in these systems possess the same proportions of FW: 
SS as above, the only difference is that substrates have already gone 
through the aerobic pre-treatment. 250 mL Schott Duran bottle was used 
as the digester in this study. The organic loading rate (OLR) of each 
reactor was set to 4 g VS/L/d with the hydraulic reaction time (HRT) of 
16 days. The working volume of the reactor was 100 mL, including 35 
mL inoculum. Bottling operation once finished, the cap was inserted 
using silicone gel plug immediately and blown under a nitrogen atmo­
sphere for 5 min to remove the oxygen (2 mL/s). After that, the reactor 
was maintained in a mesophilic temperature (37.5 ◦C) shaker at a speed 
of 150 rpm. The control reactor was filled with 35 mL inoculum and 65 
mL distilled water to exclude the background CH4 yield of the inoculum. 
12.5 mL substrate was extracted and introduced every day by using a

monitored to figure out its composition. All the data includes the 
average values. When the CH4 production was steady, the anaerobic 
digestion experiment was stopped. 
2.4. Analytical methods 
2.4.1. Chemical analysis 
The pH was measured by a pH meter (LeicipHS-3E, REX, China) 
equipped with temperature compensation. TS, VS, NH4
+-N and TKN were 
analyzed by standard methods (APHA, 2005). Crude protein content was 
determined by multiplying Kjeldahl Nitrogen (KN) amount by the factor 
6.25 [21]. Lipids were extracted with petroleum ether and quantified by 
measuring the mass loss of the residue after combustion [22]. The solute 
protein concentration and the solute carbohydrate concentration were 
determined by the Lowry method [23] and the phenol-sulfuric acid 
method [24], respectively. Elemental analyzer (Vario EL III, Elementar, 
Germany) was utilized for ultimate analysis adopting carbon-hydrogen- 
nitrogen model. 
2 mL extract was extracted from each reactor every day and centri­
fuged at 13,500 rpm for 10 min and the supernatant was filtered with a 
0.45 μm membrane filter (Millipore, USA) for the analysis of volatile 
fatty acids (VFAs), the rest was estimated for other parameters. For the 
detailed methods of sampling for VFAs, refer to Zhang et al. [25]. Gas 
chromatograph (GC-7900, TECHCOMP, Shanghai) with a thermal con­
ductivity detector (TCD) and column packed TDX-01, was used to 
determine the volume of CH4, CO2 and N2. Temperatures of injection 
port, column oven and detector were set to 100, 80, 100 ◦C, respectively. 
VFAs were also measured in the same GC-7900 equipped with a flame 
ionization detector (FID) coupled to a capillary column (GsBP-FFAP, 30 
m × 0.25 mm × 0.25 μm). The carrier gas used is Argon at a flow rate of 
44 mL/min and the split ratio was 1:20. The oven temperature was set to 
80 ◦C and for one minute, then increased to 200 ◦C at 5 ◦C/min, which 
also lasted for one minute. The temperatures of the detector and injec­
tion port were at 260 and 250 ◦C, respectively. 
2.4.2. FTIR analysis 
The organic functional groups of the substrates were measured by 
FTIR spectrometry (Nicolet 6700 Flex, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Before 
analysis, all the substrates were dewatered to consistent weight at 
105 ◦C. Solid was shredded into powder. In order to compare the in­
tensity of the peaks, the ratio of all the samples and KBr was 1:200, the 
resolution is 4 cm−1, 64 scans were collected, the wave number was 
400–4000 cm−1. 
2.4.3. Microbial community characterization 
Samples collected from systems on stable stage (66 days) were used 
for high-throughput sequencing analysis. Before analysis, the superna­
tant of samples was drained and then the remaining part was frozen at 
−20◦C. The primers of (5′-TGYCAGCCGCCGCGGTAA-3′) and Arch958­
RmodR (5′-YCCGGCGTTGAVTCCAATT-3′) were used for the polymer­
ase chain reaction (PCR) amplification of V4-V5 Archaea (Shanghai 
Majorbio Bio-Pharm Technology Co. Ltd., China). PCR reactions were 
performed in triplicate 20 μL mixture containing 4 μL of 5 × FastPfu 
Buffer, 2 μL of 2.5 mM dNTPs, 0.8 μL of each primer (5 μM), 0.4 μL of 
FastPfu Polymerase, 0.2 μL of BSA, and 10 ng of template DNA under the 
following program: 95 ◦C for 3 min, 35 cycles at 95 ◦C for 30 s, 55 ◦C for 
30 s, and 72 ◦C for 45 s, and a final extension at 72 ◦C for 10 min. 
3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Effects of simple pre-aeration on the semi-continuous anaerobic 
digestion process 
3.1.1. Production of CH4 
The daily volumetric CH4 production rate and CH4 yield profiles are 
displayed in Fig. 1(a) and (b), including different ratios of FW:SS with 
and without pre-treatment. The experiment was conducted for a total 
number of 66 days. The CH4 productivity and CH4 yield were almost 
kept stable for this duration and they were distinctly different among the 
reactors with or without pre-aeration. During the start-up period (1–9 
day), as the running time increases, CH4 production of Pre-R2, R2, Pre- 
R3, R3 from zero climbed to 796.1, 407.8, 856.5, 433.5 mL/L⋅day, 
respectively. The reason why lower production of CH4 in the primary 
stage is that, at start-up stage microbial physiological metabolic activity 
is low, thus leading to the volatility of the system. The total CH4 yield 
and productivity in current study were lower than others, due to the 
short HRT (16 days) and only 35 mL inoculum was introduced into each 
reactor. In similar studies, the ratio of inoculum: substrate was 3 times 
higher than this [26,27]. After the start-up period, the systems is in 
stable state, at this stage, stable CH4 productivity and CH4 yield were 
obtained. That is, CH4 productivity of Pre-R2 and Pre-R3 kept at 800 
mL/L⋅day, while that of R2 and R3 were 450 mL/L⋅day. With the 
exception of pre-aeration treatment, Pre-R2 and R2 were operated under 
the same conditions, but, the CH4 production was absolutely different. 
The CH4 productivity of R2 was almost twice lower than that of Pre-R2. 
Similar result was existed in Pre-R3 and R3. It could be seen that pre- 
aeration is beneficial to the CH4 production. Nevertheless, FW:SS ratio 
of feed substrate in R2 and R3 or Pre-R2 and Pre-R3 were different, but, 
the CH4 production in R2 and R3 or Pre-R2 and Pre-R3 are basically the 
same, indicating that under the same OLR, ratios of FW:SS = 1:1 and 3:1

did not exhibit significant difference on the CH4 yield. 
Fig. 2(a) revealed that Pre-R1 and R1 did not show the predominant 
performance of CH4 production when food waste was the only feed 
substrate. Fig. 2(b) and (c) illustrated the pH and VFAs of Pre-R1 and R1, 
VFAs accumulation exceed 7000 mg/L and the pH value was below 6.0 
at the third day. The high VFAs concentration caused the inhibition of 
methanogenesis [28]. Lay et al. [29] assumed that the anaerobic 
digestion process would fail if pH was lower than 6.1. Combined with 
Fig. 1, it can be proved that co-digestion is an effective method for 
treatment of FW. Without pretreatment or mixing with other wastes, the 
food waste, alone, cannot run successfully at a high OLR. So, the Pre-R1 
and R1 process was stopped when no more CH4 was produced at 22 
days. It is worth noting that though it was hard to carry out complete 
anaerobic digestion of only food waste, the gas production of the Pre-R1 
is higher than that of the untreated system (R1), since it produced CH4 
until 22 days. It demonstrated that after pre-aeration process, the pro­
duction of CH4 could be improved even though the single anaerobic 
digestion of FW, i.e., aerobic pre-treatment in the process is very 
beneficial to generate more energy. In the anaerobic digestion process of 
MSW, Ni et al. [18] found accumulated biogas production can also be 
effectively improved with 8-days short-term pre-aeration. 
Produced CH4 content was, a reflection of the activities of hydro­
lyzing bacteria, acidogens and methanogens [30]. Fig. 3 shows higher 
CH4 content in pretreated group in 66 days, which means pre-aeration 
increased the methanogenic activity. Xu et al. [31] reported that 
greater than 40% CH4 content is required for the biogas to be technically 
or economically feasible. In this study, CH4 content was maintained over 
60%, representing the high quality of originated biogas. 
From the Fig. 1, it displayed that the pre-treatment truly enhanced 
the yield of CH4, since the CH4 productivity was 60% higher for pre- 
treated array as compared to un-treated ones at the end of the opera­
tion period. In addition, co-digestion is a reliable approach to strengthen 
the performance of the anaerobic digestion of FW. The ratios (3:1 or 1:1) 
of FW:SS did not have a significant influence on the CH4 yield or its 
productivity. It means with the appropriate ratio of FW:SS, the CH4 
productivity is independent of substrate composition under the same VS. 
Therefore, in this study, FW:SS = 3:1, with 6-days pre-aeration, is a 
preferred choice when considering the efficiency of food waste disposal 
and CH4 production. 
3.1.2. The trend of pH and VFAs in the process of anaerobic digestion 
The pH value, TVFA concentration throughout the anaerobic diges­
tion process and NH4
+-N concentration after the pre-aeration are shown 
in Fig. 4. pH value is an important parameter to judge whether the 
reactor is operating normally. Fig. 4(a) showed high pH values above 7.6 
were observed at the beginning of the anaerobic digestion process, and 
then, pH decreased in all runs due to the fast conversion to acids of 
substrates. The final pH maintained within the range of 7.05–7.40 on 
stable stage. Pre-R3 had the considerably higher pH (7.35), compared to 
Pre-R2 (7.15), R2 (7.08) and R3 (7.15), those pHs were desirable for 
anaerobic digestion process [32]. The decrease of pH 20 days at the 
start-up time of the reaction could be contributed by two reasons. One is 
the activity of methanogen was low at beginning, hence, the acids were 
not fully converted to methane. Another reason is the low buffer ca­
pacity of the substrate, which led to the accumulated acids were not able 
to be balanced in time. pH values are consistent with the trend of the 
TVFA. A high TVFA was observed in the first 20 days (shown in Fig. 4 
(b)), but, with the rapid growth of methanogens, the accumulated acid 
was gradually utilized by methanogens. They were all below the inhi­
bition concentrations. Concentrations of acetate, propionate, iso-

Butyrate, n-Butyrate, iso-Valerate were also measured in Fig. 5. It is 
worth noting that N-Valerate was not detected all the time. All of them 
were at low values after start-up time. Fig. 4(c) shows the NH4

centrations of feed substrates in anaerobic digestion process. After pre- 
aeration treatment, NH4
+-N concentrations in the substrates were 
higher than non-pretreated arrays. NH4
+-N concentrations were 190, 
159, 295 and 843 mg/L for R2, R3, Pre-R2 and Pre-R3, respectively. 
Ammonium was mainly generated by protein degradation in substrate, 
which could be used to buffer the VFAs produced in the subsequent 
anaerobic digestion process and improve the CH4 production. Aerobic 
pre-treatment greatly enhanced the degradation of protein in advance 
and released NH4
+-N into bulk liquid, corresponding to the first higher 
pH values in Pre-R2 and Pre-R3. Rajagopal [33] reported that low NH4
+- 
N concentration may cause low CH4 yield, in accordance with the non- 
pre-aeration arrays which showed lower CH4 productivity. However, it 
was suggested that when NH4
+-N concentration reached to 1500 mg/L, 
an inhibition of methanogen activity would occur [34]. In this study, 
NH4
+-N concentrations of systems were all below the 1500 mg/L, thus, 
pre-treatment series with high NH4
+-N could dilute the generated VFAs 
and did not inhibit the CH4 production. In previous studies, Ni et al. [18] 
demonstrated that a suitable pre-aeration duration was critical for the 
dry anaerobic digestion of MSW by reducing the organics and providing 
a buffer to neutralize the excessive produced VFAs. 
These results, once again, suggested that the simple pre-aeration is 
an effective method for co-digestion of FW and SS. After 6-days aeration 
pre-treatment, higher pH and NH4
+-N concentration of substrates were 
observed, which are favorable for methanogens. Thus dramatically 
creating effective conditions for the stabilization and CH4 production in 
the mesophilic food waste anaerobic digestion process. 
3.2. The organic distribution of different substrates 
FW:SS = 3:1 is a preferred choice, therefore, this ratio was opted to 
determine the influence of pretreatment and non-pretreatment on the 
distribution of organic matter in the substrate. Protein and carbohydrate 
were the main components of substrate and played an important role in 
the growth of microorganisms in the system. However, the fermentation 
of microorganisms only use the solute organic components in the liquid 
phase, the content of solute proteins and carbohydrate in the fermen­
tation system were critical to the efficiency of acid production, they are 
more easily solubilized, absorbed into the cells of microorganism and 
metabolized [35,36]. Solute protein and carbohydrate of substrates 
were detected in Fig. 6. The concentration of solute protein was 256 and 
350 mg/L in the untreated and pretreated groups, respectively. The 
solute carbohydrate concentration was 198 and 667 mg/L, respectively. 
It was demonstrated that pretreatment promoted the following anaer­
obic digestion by converting macromolecular organic matter into 
available dissolved organic matter. High rates of organic matter degra­
dation could be achieved by aerobic operation [37,38]. Considering that 
hydrolysis as the limited step in the single-phase anaerobic digestion 
process, pre-aeration promoted the CH4 production by completing the 
partial hydrolysis stage in advance. 
Further investigation by FTIR analysis was carried out after drying 
the pretreated and non-pretreated substrate, as shown in Fig. 7. The 
peak appeared in several wavelengths of the sample, which indicated 
the complexity of the mixture of FW and SS. At the same time, the peak 
position of untreated and pretreated samples was similar, which sug­
gested that analogous functional groups existed in the untreated and 
pretreated reactors. The peak at wave number 1600–1700 cm−1 was 
related to N–H bending band of amide-I [39]. It was noted that the peak 
intensity at 1600–1700 cm−1 increased after aerobic pretreatment, 
indicating that aerobic pretreatment accelerated the degradation of 
proteins. The band at 1000–1190 cm−1 was the vibration of C–O, C–OH 
and C–C in carbohydrates, aromatic ethers and polysaccharides, 
respectively, which was related to the carbohydrate and aromatic ether 
substances [40]. After aerobic pretreatment, the peak weakened, which 
implied that aerobic pretreatment could promote the decomposition of 
carbohydrates into small molecules, thus reducing the content of car­
bohydrates in the substrate. 
In general, some macromolecular organic substances in the substrate 
were broken down into small molecules before anaerobic digestion. The 
introduction of aerobic pretreatment fundamentally changed the struc­
ture of functional groups of substrates, thereby, promoting the biode­
gradability of the substrates [41]. Even under the same load in the 
anaerobic digestion step, it laid an excellent environment for metha­
nogens and remarkably amended the CH4 growth rate, compared with 
the group without pretreatment.

3.3. Evolution of function microorganisms 
In order to understand the influence of pretreatment and FW:SS ratio 
on methanogenic community in the operation system, 16S RNA was 
used to measure the community structure difference of Archaea in 
different reactors at the stable stage. The Archaea community structure 
of systems at genus level was presented in Fig. 8. Methanosarcina are 
found as the major methanogen, with a high abundance of more than 
60%. In addition, there are Methanobacterium, Methanosaeta, Meth­
anofollis, Methanomassiliicoccus, Methanospirillum, etc. Total relative 
abundance of these methanogenic Archaea is over 98%. Among them, 
Methanosarcina can use methyl compounds such as acetate, H2/CO2, 
methanol and methylamine to form CH4. Therefore, it has strong 
adaptability and is a mixed methanogen, which is regarded as the 
dominant strain in anaerobic digestion process. In a stable anaerobic 
digestion reactor, Methanosarcina generally occupies the main position, 
which can be up to more than 70% [42,43]. Methanosaeta is a specific 
acetotrophic methanogen while Methanobacterium is a hydrogen- 
utilizing group. Moreover, Methanospirillum is a type of facultative 
acetate-utilizing group methanogen, Methanofollis only use hydrogen, 
carbon dioxide and formate to produce CH4 while Methanomassiliicoccus 
metabolizes mixed nutrient (methyl and hydrogen) for CH4 production.

The distribution of relative abundance of Archaea has changed 
greatly under the long-term operation of pretreated and untreated 
substrates. As can be seen from the Fig. 8, in the system without pre­
treatment, the abundance of Methanosarcina in R2 was lower than that of 
pretreatment, and the abundance of Methanosarcina in Pre-R3 and Pre- 
R2 was 93.10% and 95.98%, respectively. While the abundance in R2 
was only 62.22%, and Methanobacterium accounted for 32.57% in R2. It 
was found that Methanosarcina was mainly present in the stable opera­
tion, while Methanobcterium accounted for a small proportion. The less 
dominance of Methanosarcina resulted in lower CH4 production in un­
treated group than that in pretreated group. This result was consistent 
with Sang’s study [44], high CH4 production was observed in the 
intermittently aerated reactor, where Methanosarcinales as acetate- 
utilizing methanogens, were dominant Archaea. Compared with 
different FW:SS ratios, the abundance of Methanosarcina in Pre-R3 was 
lower than that in Pre-R2, but it was noted that compared with Pre-R2, 
Methanosaeta in Pre-R3 was 3.02%, thereby, making up for the defi­
ciency of Methanosarcina, as acetate-utilizing methanogen. 
To sum up, after aerobic pretreatment, the substrate entered the 
anaerobic system, which would change the abundance of different 
methanogens in the system. Methanogens in aerobic pretreatment group 
were mainly Methanosarcina, while methanogens in non-pretreatment 
group were mainly Methanosarcina and Methanobacterium. As a result, 
the main pathway in pre-aerated arrays was acetotrophy for methano­
genesis and methanogenic performance for non-pre-treatment group 
was weaker than that of pretreatment group. 
4. Conclusions 
The effect of 6-days aerobic pretreatment on co-digestion of FW and 
SS was studied. The results showed that aerobic pretreatment could 
increase the concentration of ammonia nitrogen in the substrate, which 
effectively buffer the acid produced and promote the CH4 production. 
After aerobic pretreatment, the maximum CH4 production capacity of 
the system was 856 mL/L day, and the VFAs concentration remained at 
low level after the successful start-up of the system. Furthermore, after 
the aerobic pretreatment, macromolecular organic matter (protein and 
carbohydrate) could be degraded into soluble protein and carbohydrate 
for utilization by fermentation microorganisms. At the same time, high- 
throughput sequencing showed that with the long-term operation of the 
reaction, the microbial community in the system altered due to the pre- 
aeration. In the aerobic pretreatment group, the methanosarcina was the 
main microorganism, while the non-pretreatment group contained 
32.57% methanobacteria. These results demonstrated that a short pre-
